title: Discount gambit: why refusing to discount (and locking in rates instead) builds a better business
summary: Jason Cohen argues that "act now" discounts breed mistrust, invite endless haggling, attract the worst customers and signal a weak brand. Instead, announce a coming price increase and offer to lock in the current rate, which protects customers, implies growth and builds loyalty.

principles.text: Offer price-lock protection against a future increase instead of a discount for acting now.
principles.quote: The price is going up, but if you buy now I will lock in your rate.

principles.text: A discount reveals the original price included padding, which breeds customer mistrust.
principles.quote: Thus #1 breeds mistrust--the opposite of what you're trying to establish with me, your customer.

principles.text: Discounting teaches buyers there's no price floor, turning the relationship into an adversarial haggle.
principles.quote: Meanwhile your "customer relationship" is now more of a "hostage situation."

principles.text: Inconsistent pricing is unfair once word gets around, and can cost you the large follow-on order.
principles.quote: Yet another problem with discounting--word gets around, meaningless differences in pricing is unfair, and now I, the customer, see you as plain old dishonest.

principles.text: Not discounting signals market leadership; discounting signals desperation to hit numbers.
principles.quote: The leader doesn't have to compromise. The leader isn't desperate for orders.

principles.text: Discount-driven offers attract the least valuable customers and repel the best, while weakening the brand.
principles.quote: Strategy #1 attracts the least-valuable customers and repels the best ones, while establishing a weak brand.
